title: DOAH 26-0048 Recommended Order: TYKEAL GALERY vs. JAMES BRODICK
text:
STATE OF FLORIDA
DIVISION OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
TYKEAL GALERY,
Petitioner,
vs. Case No. 26-0048
REALTY PROS ASSURED, LLC; AND
JAMES BRODICK,
Respondents.
/
RECOMMENDED ORDER
Pursuant to notice, a final hearing was conducted on March 13, 2026, via
Zoom before Garnett W. Chisenhall, a duly designated Administrative Law
Judge of the Division of Administrative Hearings (“DOAH”).
APPEARANCES
For Petitioner: Tykeal Galery, pro se
399 Smithfield Street
Dillonvale, Ohio 43917
For Respondent: Sven L. Smith, Esquire
Mahshie & Decosta, P.A.
900 West Granada Boulevard, Suite 3
Ormond Beach, Florida 32174
STATEMENT OF THE ISSUE
Whether the Florida Fair Housing Act (“the Act”) was violated on May 29,
2025, during a telephone conversation between Petitioner and Respondent
James Brodick.

PRELIMINARY STATEMENT
On September 28, 2025, Petitioner (“Tykeal Galery”) filed a Housing
Discrimination Complaint with the Florida Commission on Human Relations
(“the Commission”) setting forth the following allegations:
Complainant Tykeal Galery is in the process of
selling his home. As such, [Mr. Galery] belongs to a
class of persons whom [the Act] protects from
unlawful discrimination by virtue of Race.
[Mr. Galery] owns a home located at 600 Holmes
Avenue Daytona Beach, FL 32115. Respondent
James Brodick was identified by [Mr. Galery] as the
realtor that works for Respondent Realty Pros
Assured, LLC.
[Mr. Galery] alleged that on May 13, 2025,
Respondent James Brodick sent a text message that
“some people are scared of that neighborhood” and
he would not live at the subject property with his
children due to poorly rated schools in the area.
[Mr. Galery] alleged that on May 29, 2025, he had a
showing of the subject property with a potential
buyer, who is Black. [Mr. Galery] also alleged that
on May 29, 2025, Respondent James Brodick sent a
text message to ask “what color are they?” in
reference to the potential buyer. Respondent James
Brodick also texted that “that’s a good place for them
to be: after [Mr. Galery] confirmed that the person
that viewed the subject property was Black. [Mr.
Galery] alleged that on June 6, 2025, he sent a letter
to request the termination of the Real Estate
Agreement with Respondent James Brodick and
Respondent Realty Pros Assured, LLC. [Mr. Galery]
believes that Respondent James Brodick was
steering only Black potential buyers towards
viewing his home. As such, [Mr. Galery] believes
that the Respondents have subjected him to
discriminatory terms, conditions, privileges, or
services, discrimination in
terms/conditions/privileges relating to sale, and
steering due to race.
2

On December 23, 2025, the Commission issued a Notice concluding that
"reasonable cause does not exist to believe that a discriminatory housing
practice has occurred.” Mr. Galery responded by filing a Petition for Relief,
and the Commission referred this matter to DOAH on January 5, 2026.
The undersigned issued a Notice on January 20, 2026, scheduling the
final hearing for March 13, 2026.
On March 4, 2026, Mr. Galery filed a “Motion for Pre-Hearing
Stipulations” asserting “[t]his case concerns the statements made during the
May 29, 2025 telephone call between [Mr. Galery] and Respondent Brodick.”
The undersigned denied the Motion for Pre-Hearing Stipulations via an
Order issued on March 11, 2026. In doing so, the undersigned noted that “at
the outset of the final hearing, the undersigned will question the parties
about narrowing the scope of the evidentiary presentations to an alleged
phone call that occurred on May 29, 2025.”
The final hearing was convened as scheduled. At the outset, the
undersigned announced that the parties’ dispute was limited to a May 29,
2025, phone call between Mr. Galery and Mr. Brodick. Accordingly, the
undersigned elected to only accept Respondent’s Exhibit 2 into evidence.
Mr. Galery testified on his own behalf, and Respondents presented testimony
from Mr. Brodick.
The one-volume final hearing Transcript was filed on April 3, 2026.
Both parties filed timely Proposed Recommended Orders that were
considered in the preparation of this Recommended Order.
Unless stated otherwise, all references shall be to the 2024 version of the
Florida Statutes. See McClosky v. Dep’t of Fin. Serv., 115 So. 3d 441 (Fla. 5th
3

DCA 2013) (standing for the proposition that a proceeding is governed by the
law in effect at the time of the commission of the acts alleged to constitute a
violation of law).
FINDINGS OF FACT
Based on the oral and documentary evidence adduced at the final hearing,
the entire record of this proceeding, and matters subject to official
recognition, the following Findings of Fact are made:
1. Realty Pros Assured, LLC (“Realty Pros”) is a Florida real estate
brokerage, and Mr. Brodick is a licensed Florida sales associate affiliated
with Realty Pros.
2. Mr. Galery identifies as a Native American and an African American.
3. In April of 2025, Mr. Galery retained Realty Pros to assist with the sale
of his home in Daytona Beach, Florida. The sales price began at $225,000.
On April 21, 2025, the price was lowered to $216,900, and it was lowered
again on May 14, 2025, to $214,000.
4. On May 29, 2025, two different prospective buyers toured Mr. Galery’s
home. After the tours had been completed, Mr. Galery and Mr. Brodick had a
telephone conversation. According to Mr. Galery, Mr. Brodick inquired about
the prospective buyers’ race, and Mr. Galery interpreted that question to be
an indication that Mr. Brodick believed the home was inappropriate for
Caucasians. Mr. Brodick claims he was merely attempting to ascertain the
identity of an agent who had accompanied one of the buyers.
5. While there is no evidence indicating that Mr. Galery’s version of the
May 29, 2025, telephone conversation is not truthful, the undersigned is
unable to find that Mr. Galery’s version is more credible that Mr. Brodick’s.
6. Mr. Galery ultimately sold his home in October of 2025 for $176,500.
7. During the final hearing, Mr. Galery was unable to identify how he was
harmed by any actions or omissions by Mr. Brodick. For example, Mr. Galery
4

did not testify that he was forced to accept a lower price for his home due to
any actions or omissions by Mr. Brodick.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
8. DOAH has jurisdiction over the parties to and the subject matter of this
proceeding. § 120.57(1), Fla. Stat.
9. The Act, sections 760.20 through 760.37, Florida Statutes, prohibits
discrimination in matters, pertaining to a dwelling, on the basis of a person’s
race. The Act is patterned after Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, as
amended by the Fair Housing Act of 1988, and discrimination covered under
the Act is the same discrimination prohibited under the Federal Fair Housing
Act. Savannah Club Worship Serv., Inc. v. Savannah Club Homeowners’
Ass’n, Inc., 456 F. Supp. 2d 1223, 1224 n.1 (S.D. Fla. 2005). When “a Florida
Statute is modeled after a federal law on the same subject, the Florida
statute will take on the same constructions as placed on its federal prototype,
insofar as such interpretation is harmonious with the spirit and policy of the
Florida legislation.” Brand v. Fla. Power Corp., 633 So. 2d 504, 509 (Fla. 1st
DCA 1994).
10. In the instant case, Mr. Galery has the burden of establishing, by a
preponderance of the evidence, that a violation of the Act occurred.
§ 760.34(5), Fla. Stat.; Fla. Dep’t of Transp. v. J.W.C. Co., 396 So. 2d 778
(Fla. 1st DCA 1981).
11. Before assessing the merits of Mr. Galery’s discrimination claim, the
undersigned must assess whether Mr. Galery has standing. Even though
Respondents did not argue that Mr. Galery lacks standing, the undersigned
still has an obligation to make that determination. See generally Fla. Ass’n of
Med. Equip. Dealers v. Apfel, 194 F.3d 1227, 1230 (11th Cir. 1999)(stating
that “every court has an independent duty to review standing as a basis for
jurisdiction at any time, for every case it adjudicates.”); AT&T Mobility, LLC
v. Nat’l Ass’n of Stock Car Auto Racing, Inc., 494 F.3d 1356, 1360 (11th Cir.
5

2007)(stating that “we are obliged to consider standing sua sponte even if the
parties have not raised the issue because an appellate court must satisfy
itself not only of its own jurisdiction, but also of that of the lower courts in a
cause under review.”).
12. The plain language of the Act appears to require that a petitioner
must have suffered, or is about to suffer, an injury prior to filing a housing
discrimination claim. § 760.34(1), Fla. Stat. (providing that “[a]ny person who
claims to have been injured by a discriminatory housing practice or who
believes that he or she will be injured by a discriminatory housing practice
that is about to occur may file a complaint with the [C]ommission.”)(emphasis
added). See also Herbozo and Liesenfeld v. Fernandez, 2026 WL 706678, at *3
(M.D. Fla. 2026)(noting that “[a]lthough standing under the Fair Housing Act
is notoriously broad, it almost certainly does not stretch so far as to allow
plaintiffs to assert claims for alleged discrimination in apartment complexes
that they do not live in or seek to live in.”); Wheatley Heights Neighborhood
Coal. v. Jenna Resales Co., 429 F. Supp. 486, 489 (E.D. N.Y. 1977)(concluding
the plaintiffs had standing to maintain a Fair Housing Act claim based on
allegations that plaintiffs suffered the following injuries: “they do not reside
in a racially stable community, they find it more difficult to sell their homes
because defendants steer prospective white purchasers away from Wheatley
Heights, and their property values will decline should these practices
continue.”).
13. In his Housing Discrimination Complaint and Petition for Relief,
Mr. Galery does not allege that he was injured, in any way, by any actions or
omissions by Mr. Brodick. During the final hearing, Mr. Galery was unable to
answer whether any of Mr. Brodick’s actions or omissions impaired his ability
to sell his home for his desired price. As a result, the undersigned concludes
that Mr. Galery lacks standing because there is no evidence that he has been
injured by a discriminatory housing practice.
6

14. In addition, even if Mr. Galery had set forth allegations indicating that
he had been injured by a discriminatory housing practice, he failed to
demonstrate, by a preponderance of the evidence, that Respondents violated
the Act.
15. Mr. Galery’s allegations amount to a claim of racial steering. The U.S.
Supreme Court has defined “racial steering” as “directing prospective home
buyers interested in equivalent properties to different areas according to
their race.” Gladstone Realtors v. Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91, (1979).
16. Relevant portions of section 760.23(2), (3), and (4) provide that:
(2) It is unlawful to discriminate against any person
in the terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or
rental of a dwelling, or in the provision of services or
facilities in connection therewith, because of race,
color, national origin, sex, handicap, familial status
or religion.
(3) It is unlawful to make, print, or publish, or cause
to be made, printed, or published, any notice,
statement, or advertisement with respect to the sale
or rental of a dwelling that indicates any preference,
limitation, or discrimination based on race, color,
national origin, sex, disability, familial status, or
religion or an intention to make any such preference,
limitation, or discrimination.
(4) It is unlawful to represent to any person because
of race, color, national origin, sex, disability, familial
status, or religion that any dwelling is not available
for inspection, sale, or rental when such dwelling is
in fact so available.
17. Section 760.25(2)(a) provides that
[i]t is unlawful for any person or entity whose
business includes engaging in residential real estate
transactions to discriminate against any person in
making available such a transaction, or in the terms
or conditions of such a transaction, because of race,
color, national origin, sex, disability, familial status,
or religion.
7

18. Section 760.25(2)(b) defines “residential real estate transaction” to
include “[t]he selling, brokering, or appraising of residential real property.”
19. Because the undersigned did not find that Mr. Galery’s description of
the May 29, 2025, telephone conversation was more credible than
Mr. Brodick’s, Mr. Galery did not prove that Respondents violated the Act.
RECOMMENDATION
Based on the foregoing Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, it is
RECOMMENDED that the Florida Commission on Human Relations issue a
final order dismissing Tykeal Galery’s Housing Discrimination Complaint
DONE AND ENTERED this 29th day of April, 2026, in Tallahassee, Leon
County, Florida.

NOTICE OF RIGHT TO SUBMIT EXCEPTIONS
All parties have the right to submit written exceptions within 15 days from
the date of this Recommended Order. Any exceptions to this Recommended
Order should be filed with the agency that will issue the Final Order in this
case.
